phonemes.desc: Voiced alveolar stop [d] plus close back rounded vowel [u]; the Sumerian word dumu means 'son'.
Bilabial nasal [m] plus close back rounded vowel [u]; the second syllable carries the reconstructed stress.
Voiced alveolar fricative [z] plus voiceless dental stop [d]; zid means 'true, faithful, right' — the ethical core of the name.

pronunciation.approximation: 'doo-MOO-zid' — the first two syllables are soft and round, the last closes crisply like 'zid'.

pronunciation.note: Dumuzid is Tier 2: the canonical restoration uses plain Latin letters with no distinctive diacritic or non-ASCII letter. The Sumerian cuneiform signs carry meanings — dumu 'son' and zid 'faithful' — that the Latin form cannot display; it is therefore a readable scholarly transliteration rather than a phonological reconstruction.

domains.title: The Faithful Son
domains.subtitle: Shepherds, Vegetation, and the Sacred Marriage
domains.lead:
Dumuzid is the Sumerian shepherd made divine — the 'faithful son' whose name joins dumu ('son') and zid ('true, faithful, right'). He is the lord of the sheepfold, the provider of milk and wool, and the bridegroom of Inanna in the sacred marriage that guarantees the land's fertility. Unlike the storm-gods who rule by force, Dumuzid reigns through the gentle goods of the pasture: grass, water, flock, and the cyclic return of vegetation.

His myth is also the myth of seasonal loss. In the Descent of Inanna he is chosen to take the goddess's place in the underworld for half the year, so that life and death may alternate on earth. Dumuzid is therefore not only the patron of shepherds but the archetype of the dying-and-rising vegetation god, mourned as Tammuz across the ancient Near East.

cards.name: Lord of the Sheepfold
cards.desc: Patron of shepherds, milk, cheese, and wool; the pastoral economy of Sumer consecrated in one figure.

cards.name: Date Palm and Garden
cards.desc: His wedding songs praise the date palm, the garden, and the sprouting reed — the green world as bridal gift.

cards.name: Sacred Marriage
cards.desc: The union of Dumuzid and Inanna legitimates kingship and assures fertility; every New Year reenacts their cosmic wedding.

cards.name: Descent and Return
cards.desc: Half the year in the underworld, half on earth with his sister Geshtinanna — the seasonal cycle made myth.

mythology.lead: Dumuzid's myths are woven through the great Sumerian literary corpus: courtship songs, sacred-marriage hymns, the Descent of Inanna, and the laments for his death. They turn on the tension between abundance and loss, intimacy and exile, the green world and the dark earth.

myths.title: The Shepherd and the Farmer
myths.text: In the Sumerian poem Dumuzi and Enkimdu (ETCSL 4.08.33), Inanna must choose between Dumuzid, the shepherd, and Enkimdu, the farmer. The shepherd boasts of milk, cheese, and wool; the farmer counters with grain, bread, and beer. Inanna prefers Dumuzid, and the poem dramatizes the prestige of the pastoral economy alongside agriculture in early Mesopotamia.

myths.title: The Bridal of Heaven and Earth
myths.text: The sacred-marriage songs (ETCSL 4.08.01–04) celebrate Dumuzid as the bridegroom of Inanna. The king of Uruk embodies Dumuzid, while the goddess embodies the city and the land. Their union is not merely symbolic: it guarantees the me of fertility, the sprouting of grain, the filling of folds, and the legitimacy of the reigning king.

myths.title: Dumuzid in the Underworld
myths.text: In the Descent of Inanna (ETCSL 1.4.1), Inanna is killed in the underworld and resurrected only on condition that she send a substitute. She chooses Dumuzid, her beloved husband, because he did not mourn her. The galla demons drag him down, but his sister Geshtinanna offers to share his fate: Dumuzid will spend half the year in the underworld, Geshtinanna the other half. This is the Sumerian explanation of summer's parch and winter's return.

myths.title: The Weeping for Tammuz
myths.text: Sumerian city laments (e.g., The Death of Dumuzid, ETCSL 4.08.32) and later Akkadian tradition mourn the shepherd's death. The biblical prophet Ezekiel witnesses women 'weeping for Tammuz' at the Jerusalem temple gate (Ezekiel 8:14), a rite that travelled from Mesopotamia to the Levant. The tears are not only grief; they are a petition for the god's return and the restoration of vegetation.

syncretism: Dumuzid is the Sumerian original behind the Akkadian Tammūzu and the later West Semitic Tammuz. The Greeks knew a comparable dying-and-rising vegetation figure in Adonis; while Adonis has separate Northwest Semitic roots, the two share the same seasonal logic and were sometimes identified in later antiquity. In the Hebrew Bible, Tammuz appears as a foreign deity mourned in Jerusalem (Ezekiel 8:14), and the month Tammuz still bears his name in the Jewish calendar. Some Sumerian god-lists distinguish Dumuzid the Shepherd from Dumuzid-abzu, a chthonic or freshwater form; the traditions converged over time.
culturalLegacy: The name Tammuz outlived Mesopotamian cult by millennia. The fourth month of the Jewish calendar, Tammuz, preserves his memory, and the fast of the Seventeenth of Tammuz commemorates national calamity. In Arabic and Syriac folklore, Tammuz remained a byword for the death of vegetation and the summer drought. Modern scholarship treats Dumuzid as a classic example of the 'dying god' type alongside Osiris, Attis, and Adonis — though each figure has distinct local roots. His myth still shapes how we imagine the cycle of seasons, the return of spring, and the intimate link between divine love and agricultural fertility.
extendedMeditation:
Dumuzid is the god who must be lost so that the world can turn. His death is not punishment for a moral fault but the structural price of Inanna's return from the underworld. In choosing him, the goddess does not act out of cruelty; she acts out of the logic that life and death must alternate, that the green world must descend into darkness in order to rise again.

To meditate on Dumuzid is to meditate on the beloved thing that disappears. The pasture dries, the flock is penned, the bridegroom is taken underground — and yet the cycle guarantees return. His sister's compassion, splitting the sentence, reminds us that exile is bearable when it is shared. Dumuzid asks: what in your life must die for half a year so that the rest may live?
originalScriptNote: The name is written in Sumerian cuneiform as 𒌉𒍣 (dumu-zid), often preceded by the divine determinative 𒀭. The first sign means 'son,' the second 'true, faithful, right.' Standard Assyriology transliterates the name as Dumuzi(d), with the final -d sometimes omitted in older spellings. Because the Latin form preserves no distinctive diacritic or non-ASCII letter, it is classified as Tier 2: the restoration is the plain scholarly transliteration, readable but stripped of the visual density of the original signs.

archaeology: Cuneiform tablets from Nippur, Ur, and Uruk preserve Dumuzid's sacred-marriage songs and death laments. Neo-Assyrian and Late Babylonian copies of the Descent of Inanna and the Tammuz liturgies attest his continued cult into the first millennium BCE. The biblical witness in Ezekiel 8:14 confirms the rite's spread to Jerusalem, while the month-name Tammuz in the Jewish calendar preserves his memory into the present.
